q: Which black grape typically produces wines that are pale garnet in colour yet very high in both tannin and acidity?
exp: Nebbiolo (Barolo, Barbaresco) is deceptive: pale in the glass but powerfully tannic and acidic, with tar and rose aromas.

q: A medium-bodied Italian red with red cherry, dried herbs and high acidity is most likely made from:
exp: That is the classic Sangiovese profile — the grape of Chianti and Brunello di Montalcino.

q: Which Piedmont grape is prized for everyday reds with very high acidity but gentle tannins?
exp: Barbera's high acid and low-to-medium tannin make it a juicy, food-friendly counterpart to austere Nebbiolo.

q: A simple Valpolicella made from Corvina is typically:
exp: Unfortified, non-dried Corvina makes light, fresh, cherry-scented reds. Only appassimento (Amarone) makes it powerful.

q: Which grape is the main variety in Amarone della Valpolicella?
exp: Corvina is the lead grape; the grapes are dried (appassimento) before fermentation to concentrate sugar and flavour.

q: Argentinian Malbec is typically:
opts: deeply coloured and full-bodied with black plum
pale and light-bodied with tart cranberry
medium-bodied with dried herbs and orange peel
exp: Malbec from Mendoza gives deep colour, plush velvety tannins and ripe black fruit.

q: Which structural profile best describes Cabernet Sauvignon?
opts: Low tannin, low acidity, ripe strawberry fruit
No tannin, high acidity, gooseberry and cut grass
High tannin, medium(+) acidity, blackcurrant fruit
Medium tannin, very high acidity, banana and kirsch
exp: Cabernet Sauvignon's thick skins give high tannin, and blackcurrant (cassis) is its signature fruit.

q: Cabernet Sauvignon grown in a cool climate or picked before full ripeness often shows:
opts: aromas of apricot, honey and ginger
green bell pepper and herbaceous notes
exp: Underripe Cabernet shows herbaceous, green bell pepper notes — a classic cool-climate marker.

q: Compared with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot generally has:
opts: softer tannins and riper, plummier fruit
higher tannin and much higher acidity
exp: Merlot ripens earlier and gives rounder, softer, plum-and-chocolate wines — the approachable half of the Bordeaux blend.

q: The classic red blend of Bordeaux combines:
exp: Cabernet brings structure and blackcurrant; Merlot brings softness and body. Cabernet Franc often plays a supporting role.

q: Which grape produces pale, high-acid reds with red cherry and strawberry and silky, low-to-medium tannins?
exp: Pinot Noir is thin-skinned, giving pale colour and gentle tannin, with red fruit that turns earthy (forest floor) with age.

q: Why is Pinot Noir considered a difficult grape to grow?
opts: Its thin skins rot easily and it needs a cool to moderate climate
It ripens so early that harvest is impossible to schedule
Its thick skins make the wines too tannic unless climates are very hot
It can only legally be planted in France
exp: Thin skins make it prone to rot and sunburn; too much heat cooks away its delicate aromas.

q: Syrah from the cool Northern Rhône typically shows:
opts: jammy raisined fruit and milk chocolate
exp: Cool-climate Syrah (Côte-Rôtie, Hermitage) is famous for black pepper and violet over fresh black fruit.

q: A typical Barossa Valley Shiraz is:
opts: full-bodied with ripe blackberry and liquorice
light-bodied with high acid and tart cranberry
pale garnet with tar and rose aromas
off-dry with orange blossom and grapes
exp: Barossa's warm climate gives concentrated, full-bodied, jammy Shiraz — the opposite pole to peppery Northern Rhône Syrah.

q: Which black grape typically gives high alcohol, soft tannins and strawberry fruit, anchoring many southern French blends?
exp: Grenache accumulates lots of sugar (= alcohol) with gentle tannin — the backbone of Châteauneuf-du-Pape and GSM blends.

q: The 'GSM' blend of the Southern Rhône and Australia stands for:
exp: Grenache gives fruit and alcohol, Syrah colour and spice, Mourvèdre tannin and meaty depth.

q: Rioja matured in American oak often shows which flavours alongside its red fruit?
exp: American oak is a Rioja tradition; it gives pronounced vanilla and coconut notes to Tempranillo.

q: Which best describes a typical Beaujolais made from Gamay?
opts: Light-bodied with low tannin and fresh red fruit
Full-bodied with high tannin and black fruit
Deeply coloured with dried fruit and chocolate
Medium-bodied with vanilla and coconut oak
exp: Gamay is light, fresh and fruity — often with banana or kirsch notes from carbonic maceration.

q: Zinfandel is genetically the same grape as:
exp: California's Zinfandel and Puglia's Primitivo are the same variety under different names.

q: White Zinfandel is best described as:
exp: White Zinfandel is a pale pink, off-dry to medium-sweet rosé made from the black Zinfandel grape.

q: Pinotage is a crossing of which two varieties?
exp: Created in South Africa in 1925, Pinotage crosses Pinot Noir with Cinsaut (then called Hermitage — hence the name).

q: Which country has made Carmenère its signature black grape?
exp: Carmenère came from Bordeaux, was long mistaken for Merlot in Chile, and is now Chile's calling card.

q: Fully ripe Carmenère typically combines black fruit with:
opts: petrol, honey and toasted bread notes
exp: Even ripe Carmenère keeps a savoury herbal/pepper edge; underripe examples are aggressively green.

q: Touriga Nacional is best known as a key grape of:
exp: Touriga Nacional leads the blend of black Douro varieties behind Port (and the valley's dry reds).

q: Why can Chardonnay be made in so many different styles?
opts: It is the only grape that ripens fully in every climate
Its thick skins allow months of maceration
It is non-aromatic and responds well to oak, lees and MLF
EU law permits blending it with any other variety
exp: As a relatively neutral grape, Chardonnay is a canvas for climate and winemaking choices — from lean Chablis to buttery Napa.

q: Chardonnay from a warm region such as Napa typically shows:
opts: gooseberry and freshly cut grass with high acidity
lean green apple and wet stone with a light body
ripe peach and tropical fruit with fuller body
light body with grapey, floral aromas
exp: Warm climates push Chardonnay toward stone and tropical fruit with more body and alcohol.

q: Which is the classic profile of Sauvignon Blanc?
opts: High acidity with gooseberry, grass and citrus
Medium acidity with butter, hazelnut and cream
Low acidity with peach, apricot and blossom
Rich gold colour with lychee and rose
exp: Sauvignon Blanc is pungently herbaceous and citrusy with mouth-watering acidity.

q: Why is Sauvignon Blanc usually fermented in stainless steel rather than new oak?
opts: because it cannot finish fermenting in barrel
because oak would turn the wine pink
to encourage a layer of flor to form
to preserve its fresh primary aromas
exp: Its appeal is vibrant primary fruit; inert vessels and cool ferments protect exactly that.

q: Bottle-aged Riesling is famous for developing:
exp: Petrol (kerosene) is the classic tertiary marker of mature Riesling, alongside honey and toast.

q: Which feature makes Riesling especially suited to both long aging and sweet styles?
exp: Riesling keeps high acidity even at full ripeness, balancing sweetness and preserving wines for decades.

q: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape. How do the classic Italian and Alsace styles differ?
opts: Italian versions are light and crisp; Alsace versions are richer, sometimes off-dry
Italian versions are rich and oily; Alsace versions are light, crisp and neutral
They are two entirely unrelated grape varieties that happen to share a name
exp: Same grape, different goals: Veneto picks early for fresh, neutral whites; Alsace goes for ripeness, body and spice.

q: Which white grape gives deeply coloured, full-bodied wines with lychee, rose and low acidity?
exp: Gewurztraminer's pink skins give golden colour, and its hallmark is intense lychee/rose perfume with low acid and high alcohol.

q: Viognier, the grape of Condrieu, is typically:
opts: light and tart with green apple and flint
neutral and saline with searing acidity and a light body
full-bodied with apricot, blossom and low acidity
grassy and herbaceous with light body
exp: Viognier is the rare aromatic white with LOW acidity — perfumed, rich and oily in texture.

q: Which white grape has searingly high acidity and makes dry, sweet and sparkling wines in the Loire?
exp: Chenin Blanc's acidity supports every style — bone-dry Savennières, sweet Vouvray, and sparkling Crémant de Loire.

q: In South Africa, Chenin Blanc is traditionally known as:
exp: Steen is the local name; Chenin is South Africa's most planted variety.

q: Mature Chenin Blanc and its sweet styles often show:
opts: honey, quince and a wet-wool note
exp: Honeyed quince with a distinctive lanolin/wet-wool character is textbook aged Chenin.

q: Albariño from Rías Baixas typically shows:
opts: low acidity with butterscotch, cream and vanilla
high acidity with stone fruit and a saline note
deep gold colour with petrol and raisins
exp: Grown near the Atlantic, Albariño is fresh and citrus-and-peach driven with a sea-spray salinity — built for seafood.

q: Which grape is prone to noble rot and forms the backbone of Sauternes?
exp: Thin-skinned Sémillon takes botrytis beautifully; Sauvignon Blanc adds acidity to the blend.

q: Which variety is classically blended with Sémillon in white Bordeaux?
exp: Sauvignon Blanc brings zest and aroma; Sémillon brings body — in both dry Bordeaux Blanc and sweet Sauternes.

q: Hunter Valley Sémillon is unusual because it is:
opts: fortified with grape spirit before bottling
fermented on its skins for colour and tannin
made sweet by noble rot that develops reliably every vintage
picked early and low in alcohol, aging into toast and honey
exp: Young Hunter Semillon is lean and neutral; with a decade it transforms into honeyed, toasty complexity without any oak.

q: Furmint is the key grape of which famous sweet wine?
exp: Furmint's very high acidity and thin skins make it ideal for the botrytized Aszú wines of Tokaj, Hungary.

q: Which variety famously smells of the grape itself?
exp: Muscat (Moscato) is the rare 'grapey' grape — floral, sweet-fruited, the base of Asti.

q: Which of these white grapes is NOT considered aromatic?
exp: Chardonnay is relatively neutral — its character comes largely from place and winemaking, not pungent varietal aroma.

q: Which wine would you expect to have the DEEPEST colour?
exp: Malbec is thick-skinned and inky. Gamay and Pinot Noir are pale, and Nebbiolo, despite its power, is pale garnet.

q: Which of these wines typically has the HIGHEST tannin?
exp: Barolo's Nebbiolo is among the most tannic of all grapes; Gamay and Corvina are among the least.

q: Which white typically shows the LOWEST acidity?
exp: Viognier is full-bodied and low-acid; the other three are all high-acid varieties.

q: Which black grape typically has the LIGHTEST tannin?
exp: Gamay gives light, low-tannin, chillable reds — the others are all firmly structured.

q: A dry, full-bodied white with butter, vanilla and ripe peach is most likely:
exp: Butter (MLF) + vanilla (new oak) + ripe stone fruit is the signature of a rich, warm-climate Chardonnay.

q: A pungent white with passion fruit, gooseberry and very high acidity is most likely:
opts: a Rueda Verdejo aged in oak
exp: Passion fruit layered over gooseberry and green notes is the calling card of New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc.

q: Which grape is behind the classic aged reds of Rioja, showing red cherry, leather and vanilla?
exp: Tempranillo leads Rioja blends; Garnacha and Graciano play supporting roles.

q: A full-bodied red from Pauillac with blackcurrant, cedar and firm tannins is dominated by:
exp: Pauillac sits on the gravelly Left Bank of Bordeaux, where Cabernet Sauvignon rules the blend.

q: In Australia, Syrah is known as:
exp: Same grape, different name — and typically a riper, fuller style than the Northern Rhône.

q: Verdicchio from central Italy is known for a signature finish of:
exp: A refreshing bitter-almond twist on the finish is Verdicchio's classic tell.

q: Gavi is a dry Italian white made from:
exp: Cortese makes the crisp, citrusy Gavi DOCG in Piedmont.

q: Soave is made primarily from which grape?
exp: Garganega gives Soave its pear, white pepper and light almond character in the Veneto.

q: A jammy, full-bodied Californian red with blackberry, dried fruit and sweet spice is most likely:
exp: Zinfandel ripens unevenly, so raisined berries add dried-fruit sweetness and high alcohol to the jammy profile.

q: Torrontés, Argentina's aromatic white, typically shows:
opts: deep amber colour with raisin flavours
exp: Torrontés is intensely perfumed — think rose petal and Muscat-like grapiness — usually dry on the palate.

q: Melon Blanc is the grape behind which crisp, neutral French white?
exp: Melon Blanc (Melon de Bourgogne) makes light, high-acid Muscadet near the Atlantic mouth of the Loire.

q: Chablis is best described as:
opts: lean, high-acid Chardonnay, usually without new oak
rich, buttery Chardonnay marked by new oak and vanilla
a light red made from Gamay
exp: Burgundy's northernmost outpost makes steely, green-apple Chardonnay — cool climate, little or no new oak.

q: Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet are famous for:
exp: These Côte de Beaune villages set the world benchmark for barrel-fermented, nutty, complex Chardonnay.

q: Pouilly-Fuissé comes from which part of Burgundy?
exp: The Mâconnais is Burgundy's warm southern end — Pouilly-Fuissé is its riper, fuller Chardonnay star.

q: The Côte de Nuits is famous above all for:
exp: Villages like Gevrey-Chambertin and Vosne-Romanée make the world's most sought-after Pinot Noir.

q: Pauillac and Margaux are communes of which area?
exp: Both are famous Médoc communes on the gravelly Left Bank, built around Cabernet Sauvignon.

q: Saint-Émilion and Pomerol sit on which side of Bordeaux, favouring which grape?
exp: The cooler clay soils of the Right Bank suit early-ripening Merlot, supported by Cabernet Franc.

q: Sauternes is famous for:
opts: sweet botrytized wines from Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc
structured, age-worthy reds from Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot
exp: Misty mornings off the rivers encourage noble rot, concentrating Sémillon into honeyed, apricot-rich sweet wine.

q: The Sauvignon Blancs of Sancerre are classically described as:
opts: oak-aged and buttery with ripe tropical fruit flavours
off-dry with lychee and rose petal
dry, high in acid, with citrus and flinty minerality
exp: Loire Sauvignon is the restrained, mineral pole of the grape — versus the exuberant tropical style of Marlborough.

q: Vouvray produces dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling wines, all from:
exp: Vouvray is the Loire's showcase for Chenin Blanc in every style its high acidity allows.

q: Muscadet, from the Atlantic end of the Loire, is best described as:
opts: rich, oak-aged and buttery, in the style of Meursault
light, dry and high in acid — classic with oysters
exp: Neutral Melon Blanc plus sur lie aging gives a light, fresh white made for shellfish.

q: Alsace whites are distinctive in France because they are:
exp: Unusually for France, Alsace names the grape — Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris — on the label.

q: Côte-Rôtie and Hermitage make powerful reds from:
exp: Syrah is the only permitted black grape in the Northern Rhône's steep, granite crus.

q: Condrieu is a prestigious appellation for which grape?
exp: Condrieu, in the Northern Rhône, is the world benchmark for perfumed, full-bodied Viognier.

q: Châteauneuf-du-Pape reds are typically:
opts: Cabernet and Merlot blends matured in new French oak
full-bodied, Grenache-led blends with high alcohol
exp: The Southern Rhône's flagship blends Grenache with Syrah, Mourvèdre and others into warm, spicy, powerful reds.

q: Most wine labelled Côtes du Rhône comes from:
exp: The generic appellation covers the wide southern valley — mostly Grenache-based, easy-drinking blends.

q: Fleurie and Morgon are crus of which region?
exp: The ten Beaujolais crus — Fleurie, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent among them — are the top tier of Gamay.

q: Provence is best known internationally for:
exp: Grenache-based, pale salmon, bone-dry rosé is Provence's signature export.

q: Why does the Champagne region suit sparkling wine production?
opts: its hot summers guarantee fully ripe grapes with plenty of sugar
its vineyards sit at extremely high altitude
its cool climate keeps grapes high in acid with delicate flavours
it never rains during the growing season
exp: Barely-ripe, high-acid base wine is exactly what the traditional method needs; chalk soils and cool weather deliver it.

q: Mosel Rieslings are typically:
opts: full-bodied, dry, and often matured in new oak barrels
deeply coloured, tannic and high in alcohol
light-bodied, low in alcohol, high in acid, often off-dry
exp: The Mosel's steep slate slopes barely ripen Riesling — giving featherweight, racy wines where sweetness balances acid.

q: Compared with the Mosel, Rieslings from the Rheingau tend to be:
exp: The warmer Rheingau ripens Riesling further, producing more trocken (dry) styles with more body.

q: Baden, Germany's warmest region, is noted for Spätburgunder — the German name for:
exp: Spätburgunder = Pinot Noir. Baden's warmth makes it Germany's red wine heartland.

q: Rioja reds are based primarily on:
exp: Tempranillo leads, Garnacha adds body and fruit. (Palomino and PX are the white Sherry grapes.)

q: Ribera del Duero grows Tempranillo on a high plateau, giving wines that are:
opts: deeply coloured and full-bodied with firm structure
noticeably lighter and paler than typical Rioja reds
exp: Hot days build ripeness while cold nights at ~800m preserve acidity — a more powerful expression than most Rioja.

q: Priorat's distinctive slate soils (llicorella) produce:
opts: light, spritzy whites in the style of Vinho Verde
concentrated, powerful reds from Garnacha and Cariñena
pale, delicate reds made from thin-skinned Pinot Noir grapes
sweet fortified wines from sun-dried grapes
exp: Struggling old vines on barren slate give tiny yields of intensely concentrated, full-bodied reds.

q: Rías Baixas, on Spain's Atlantic coast, is famed for:
exp: Green, rainy Galicia is white wine country — high-acid Albariño made for the local seafood.

q: Sherry can only come from the area around which Andalusian town?
exp: The Sherry triangle — Jerez, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María — sits in Spain's hot south.

q: Most Cava is produced in which region?
exp: The Penedès area near Barcelona is the heartland of traditional-method Cava.

q: Barolo and Barbaresco are made in which Italian region?
exp: Both DOCGs sit in the fog-prone hills of Piedmont, in Italy's north-west — 100% Nebbiolo.

q: Chianti is produced in which region of Italy?
exp: Chianti's Sangiovese-based reds come from the hills of central Tuscany.

q: Brunello di Montalcino is:
opts: a light, fizzy Moscato from Piedmont
a dried-grape sweet red from the Veneto
a powerful 100% Sangiovese from a warm Tuscan hill town
a long-lived Nebbiolo-based red from the hills of Piedmont
exp: Montalcino is warmer and drier than Chianti, giving fuller, long-lived, 100% Sangiovese wines.

q: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is made from which grape? (Careful!)
exp: Trap question: Montepulciano here is a Tuscan TOWN, and its wine is Sangiovese. The Montepulciano GRAPE grows in Abruzzo.

q: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is:
opts: a sparkling red from the Veneto
a Sangiovese from the Tuscan town of Montepulciano
a white wine from the Marche
a red made from the Montepulciano grape in Abruzzo
exp: Here Montepulciano is the GRAPE — soft, deeply coloured, plummy reds from Italy's Adriatic coast.

q: Soave and Valpolicella are neighbouring zones in which region?
exp: Both sit near Verona in the Veneto — Garganega whites and Corvina reds respectively.

q: Puglia, in Italy's hot south, is the home of:
exp: The heel of Italy's boot makes ripe, full-bodied Primitivo (California's Zinfandel).

q: Fiano is a quality white from which southern Italian region?
exp: Fiano makes textured, stone-fruited whites in Campania, inland from Naples.

q: Port comes from which river valley, with its steep terraces of schist?
exp: The Douro's baking-hot, steeply terraced schist slopes in northern Portugal are the source of all Port.

q: Tokaj in Hungary is world-famous for:
exp: Tokaji Aszú, from botrytized Furmint, was prized by royal courts centuries before Sauternes rose to fame.

q: Napa Valley's reputation rests above all on:
exp: Napa's warm climate produces rich, concentrated, often expensive Cabernet Sauvignon.

q: Los Carneros and the Russian River Valley stay cool thanks to:
opts: their vineyards' extreme altitude in the coastal ranges
fog and breezes drawn in from the Pacific
exp: Morning fog off San Pablo Bay and the Pacific makes these prime Californian sites for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

q: Oregon's Willamette Valley built its reputation on:
exp: Cool and rainy like Burgundy, the Willamette Valley is America's Pinot Noir heartland.

q: Washington State's Columbia Valley lies east of the Cascade mountains, so its vineyards are:
opts: among the rainiest vineyards in the world
dry and sunny, relying on irrigation
exp: The Cascades block Pacific rain (a rain shadow); long sunny days plus irrigation ripen Merlot, Cabernet and Syrah.

q: Mendoza's top vineyards, such as the Uco Valley, are planted at high altitude because:
opts: Malbec will not ripen below 1,000 metres
frost cannot occur at high elevation
vineyard land is cheaper in the mountains
cool nights preserve acidity and freshness
exp: In hot, dry Mendoza, altitude is the cooling influence — big day-night swings keep Malbec fresh and aromatic.

q: Torrontés is the signature aromatic white of:
exp: Floral, grapey Torrontés thrives in Argentina's high, sunny vineyards — especially Salta and La Rioja provinces.

q: Chile's Casablanca Valley is cooled by ocean influence and specialises in:
opts: powerful, fully ripe Carmenère and Syrah
exp: Coastal fog and breezes make Casablanca a white-wine and Pinot Noir zone; Carmenère needs warmer inland sites.

q: The Maipo Valley near Santiago is best known for:
exp: Warm, sheltered Maipo is Chile's classic source of blackcurranty, often minty Cabernet Sauvignon.

q: The Barossa Valley is celebrated for:
opts: full-bodied Shiraz from very old vines
delicate Pinot Noir and cool-climate Chardonnay
exp: Some Barossa Shiraz vines are over a century old, giving concentrated, chocolatey, full-throttle reds.

q: The Clare and Eden Valleys are Australia's benchmarks for:
opts: dry Riesling with lime and high acidity
buttery, oak-driven Chardonnay with tropical fruit
exp: These elevated South Australian valleys make bone-dry, lime-scented Riesling that ages superbly under screwcap.

q: Coonawarra's famous terra rossa soil produces outstanding:
exp: The narrow strip of red soil over limestone is Australia's signature Cabernet terroir — cassis, mint and eucalyptus.

q: Margaret River, in Western Australia's maritime climate, excels with:
opts: Nebbiolo, Barbera and other Italian varieties
exp: Ocean-moderated Margaret River is often compared to Bordeaux — premium Cabernet plus superb Chardonnay.

q: The Yarra Valley near Melbourne is a cool region noted for:
exp: One of Australia's coolest regions, the Yarra specialises in elegant Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine.

q: Marlborough, New Zealand's largest wine region, sits at the top of:
exp: Sunny, dry Marlborough occupies the north-eastern tip of the South Island.

q: Hawke's Bay, on New Zealand's warmer North Island, is known for:
exp: NZ's second-largest region is warm enough for Bordeaux-style blends and increasingly admired Syrah.

q: Central Otago, the world's southernmost wine region, is famous for:
exp: Central Otago's continental climate produces New Zealand's boldest Pinot Noir.

q: Stellenbosch is best known for:
opts: crisp white wines and nothing else
light, chillable reds made by carbonic maceration
Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinotage and other structured reds
exp: South Africa's most famous region is red wine country — Cabernet, Bordeaux blends, Shiraz and Pinotage.

q: Walker Bay, cooled by the Atlantic, is a South African home of:
exp: The cool Walker Bay/Hemel-en-Aarde area produces South Africa's most Burgundian Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

q: Vinho Verde from northern Portugal is typically:
opts: light, high-acid, low-alcohol and often gently spritzy
deeply coloured, tannic and built for long aging
sweet, fortified and served with dessert
rich, oaky and buttery, similar to white Burgundy
exp: From cool, rainy north-west Portugal — fresh, citrusy whites, often with a gentle prickle of CO₂.

q: During fermentation, yeast converts grape sugar into:
exp: Sugar → alcohol + CO₂ (+ heat). This is the fundamental reaction of all winemaking.

q: Fermentation usually stops naturally when:
opts: the cap of skins finally sinks to the bottom of the vat
all the sugar is consumed, or alcohol reaches about 15%
the grapes' acid is used up
malolactic conversion begins and displaces the yeast
exp: Yeast dies once sugar runs out or alcohol becomes toxic to it (~15% abv) — which is why table wine tops out around there.

q: Why are black grapes fermented ON their skins?
opts: EU law requires it for red wine
colour and tannin are found in the skins
skins protect the juice from oxygen
the skins contain most of the sugar
exp: Grape juice is essentially colourless — red wine gets its colour and tannin by macerating the skins during fermentation.

q: When is a typical white wine pressed?
exp: Whites are pressed off their skins first, then the clear juice is fermented — the opposite order to red wine.

q: Making rosé by 'short maceration' means:
opts: juice stays on black grape skins for only a few hours before pressing
white grapes are fermented at unusually warm temperatures on skins
finished red and white wines are blended together in the cellar
exp: A brief soak extracts just a blush of colour; the pale juice then ferments like a white wine.

q: Cool fermentation temperatures for white wines help to:
opts: keep fresh, fruity aromas in the wine
extract extra tannin from the skins
exp: Heat blows off delicate floral and fruity aromas — cool ferments (12–22°C) preserve them.

q: Malolactic conversion (MLF) changes:
opts: sharp malic acid into softer, creamier lactic acid
water into glycerol, adding an oily texture
leftover grape sugar into extra alcohol
harsh young tannins into softer colour pigments
exp: MLF softens acidity and can add butter/cream flavours — standard for reds, a stylistic choice for whites.

q: A winemaker wants a crisp, aromatic Sauvignon Blanc. Which combination fits best?
opts: extended maceration on the grape skins
drying the grapes before pressing them
stainless steel, cool fermentation, no MLF
new oak barrels, warm fermentation and full MLF
exp: Inert vessel + cool ferment + blocked MLF = maximum fresh varietal fruit and zingy acidity.

q: Aging a wine on its lees gives it:
opts: a deeper, more stable red colour
extra body plus biscuit and bread flavours
a persistent natural sparkle in the glass
exp: Dead yeast cells (lees) slowly break down, adding texture and savoury, bready complexity.

q: Fermenting or maturing in NEW oak barrels gives a wine:
opts: vanilla and clove flavours plus gentle oxygen exposure
no flavour change, only a faster and warmer fermentation
fresh banana and bubblegum aromas with softer tannins
exp: New oak contributes spice/vanilla flavours, and the porous wood lets in tiny amounts of oxygen that soften the wine.

q: Older, previously used oak barrels mainly provide:
opts: carbon dioxide for a light spritz
strong vanilla and coconut flavours, like new oak
slow oxygen exposure with little added flavour
exp: After a few uses oak gives up little flavour, but the gentle oxidative softening continues — ideal for subtle styles.

q: Which vessel adds no flavour and keeps oxygen away from the wine?
exp: Stainless steel is inert and airtight — the tool of choice for fresh, fruity styles.

q: Compared with a large old vat, a small new barrique gives:
opts: more oak flavour per litre of wine
exp: Small barrels mean more wood surface per litre — and new wood has the most flavour to give.

q: Punching down and pumping over during red fermentation both serve to:
opts: dissolve enough oxygen for the fermentation to begin
cool the fermenting must quickly and evenly through the vat
remove excess alcohol from the fermenting wine
keep the skins in contact with the juice for extraction
exp: CO₂ pushes the skins up into a floating 'cap' — it must be mixed back in or extraction stops.

q: Carbonic maceration, used in Beaujolais, gives wines with:
opts: much heavier tannin and darker colour extraction
banana and bubblegum notes and softer tannins
exp: Whole uncrushed berries ferment from within, amplifying fruity esters (banana, kirsch) while extracting little tannin.

q: Amarone is full-bodied and high in alcohol because:
opts: sugar is added to the fermenting must
its grapes are dried (appassimento) before fermentation
it is fortified with grape spirit during fermentation
its grapes are shrivelled by noble rot on the vine
exp: Weeks of drying concentrate the sugars in Corvina grapes; fermented dry, the result is powerful and raisin-tinged.

q: Which of the following is NOT a way of making sweet wine?
opts: stopping fermentation before the sugar is used up
exp: MLF changes acid character, not sweetness. The others — interrupting fermentation, botrytis, drying — are the classic routes.

q: Icewine (Eiswein) is sweet because:
opts: sugar syrup is stirred into the finished wine before bottling
the water in the grape freezes and stays behind at pressing
the juice is boiled down before fermenting
exp: Pressing naturally frozen grapes releases only concentrated sugary juice — the ice stays in the press.

q: Noble rot (botrytis) produces great sweet wine when:
opts: misty mornings are followed by warm, dry afternoons
vineyards stay damp, cool and grey for weeks on end
the grapes are picked while still unripe
exp: Humidity lets the fungus start; afternoon sun keeps it 'noble', shrivelling grapes and concentrating sugar, acid and flavour (honey, apricot, marmalade).

q: Port is sweet and Sherry is dry chiefly because:
opts: Port is fortified DURING fermentation, Sherry AFTER it
Port has sugar syrup added at bottling
Port is made from naturally sweeter grape varieties
Sherry is boiled to drive off its sugar
exp: Adding spirit mid-ferment kills the yeast and locks in Port's sugar; Sherry's base wine ferments fully dry first.

q: Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) is used throughout winemaking mainly:
opts: to add sweetness to the wine
exp: SO₂ protects wine from oxygen and spoilage organisms — used sparingly from crusher to bottling.

q: Fining and filtering are carried out to:
opts: dissolve CO₂ for a light sparkle
concentrate the wine and increase its alcohol
add extra structure and fine-grained tannin
clarify and stabilise the wine before bottling
exp: Both remove hazy particles so the wine is bright and stable in bottle.

q: Blending across vineyards, varieties or vintages is used above all to:
opts: comply with EU rules that require blending
achieve balance and a consistent style
exp: From non-vintage Champagne to GSM, blending balances the strengths of each component and keeps house styles consistent.

q: Tannin in red wine comes mostly from:
opts: the sugary pulp of the grape
the grape skins, seeds and stems
exp: Maceration extracts tannin from the solid parts of the grape; oak can add a little more later.

q: The 'cap' during red wine fermentation is:
opts: the first, finest fraction of press juice
the lid sealing the fermentation tank
the mass of skins pushed to the surface by CO₂
a layer of protective yeast on the surface
exp: Rising CO₂ floats the skins into a thick cap that must be punched down or pumped over for extraction.

q: A wine's final alcohol level is determined mainly by:
opts: how much sugar the grapes contained at harvest
how long the wine ages before release
the size and age of barrel used for maturation
exp: More sugar in = more alcohol out (unless fermentation is stopped early). Ripeness at picking sets the ceiling.

q: Most of the world's vineyards lie within which latitude bands?
opts: 0°–20° north and south of the equator
50°–70° north and south of the equator
30°–50° north and south of the equator
exp: These temperate bands offer the warmth-with-seasons balance vines need; outside them it is generally too hot or too cold.

q: To grow and ripen grapes, a vine fundamentally needs:
opts: rich, fertile soil above all else
frost in spring and wind in summer
exp: Sunlight powers photosynthesis, warmth drives ripening, and water and nutrients feed the vine — the four essentials.

q: How does a nearby large body of water affect a vineyard?
opts: it moderates temperatures, warming winters and cooling summers
it blocks sunlight from reaching the vines
it always increases the risk of spring frost
it guarantees plentiful rainfall through the growing season
exp: Water heats and cools far more slowly than land, smoothing out temperature extremes nearby.

q: In a hot country, planting vineyards at high altitude:
opts: makes the grapes ripen faster in the stronger sunshine
keeps the grapes cooler, preserving acidity and freshness
eliminates any risk of frost or hail damage
has no effect on the resulting wine
exp: Temperature drops roughly 0.6°C per 100m of elevation — altitude is the key cooling factor in Mendoza and Salta.

q: In the Northern Hemisphere, which slope aspect receives the most sun?
opts: aspect makes no difference to sunlight
exp: South-facing slopes angle toward the sun — critical for ripening in cool regions like the Mosel and Burgundy.

q: Steep slopes benefit cool-climate vineyards because they:
opts: increase the yield of each vine
make mechanical harvesting far easier and cheaper
drain water quickly and angle the vines toward the sun
trap beneficial pockets of cold air around the ripening vines
exp: Better drainage plus better sun exposure — at the cost of expensive hand labour.

q: The dark slate soils of the Mosel help ripening by:
opts: reflecting all sunlight away from the grapes
keeping the soil constantly cold and damp
absorbing heat by day and radiating it at night
adding a slate flavour directly to the wine
exp: In this marginal climate, heat stored by slate helps Riesling ripen. (Soils do not literally flavour wine!)

q: The large round stones (galets) of Châteauneuf-du-Pape:
opts: exist purely for their traditional appearance
store daytime heat and release it to the vines at night
reflect the fierce sunlight away to keep the vineyard cool
hold rainwater in pools on the surface
exp: The famous pudding stones act as storage heaters, aiding ripening of Grenache.

q: Why does gravel soil suit Cabernet Sauvignon in the Médoc?
opts: it holds water like a sponge through summer
it prevents phylloxera from attacking roots
it drains freely and warms up quickly
it is exceptionally rich in nutrients
exp: Well-drained, warm gravel helps late-ripening Cabernet reach full maturity in a marginal maritime climate.

q: Cooler, water-retaining clay soils are associated with which Bordeaux grape?
exp: Early-ripening Merlot handles cool clay well — hence its dominance on the Right Bank (Pomerol, Saint-Émilion).

q: Spring frost is dangerous in the vineyard because it:
opts: makes the grapes ripen too quickly, losing all acidity
adds unwanted sweetness to the grapes
kills the new buds and shoots, cutting the year's crop
exp: A single cold night can destroy the young growth that would have carried the entire vintage.

q: Hail during the growing season:
opts: raises the acidity of the crop
usefully improves concentration in the berries
physically damages grapes, leaves and shoots
exp: Hailstones shred canopies and split berries (inviting rot) — one of the most feared vineyard hazards.

q: Morning fog in regions like Sonoma and Casablanca:
opts: cools the vineyards, slowing ripening and preserving acidity
guarantees noble rot in every vintage
insulates the vineyard, keeping it warm through the night
exp: Fog burn-off delays the day's heat, stretching the ripening season — ideal for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc.

q: The Humboldt current (Chile) and Benguela current (South Africa) affect nearby wine regions by:
opts: cooling them with cold water and ocean breezes
warming their winters and springs significantly
bringing constant rain at harvest time
exp: Cold currents flowing from polar waters chill the coastal air, allowing fresh styles in otherwise hot countries.

q: A continental climate is defined by:
opts: the influence of a nearby warm ocean
mild temperatures with rainfall spread evenly across the year
large temperature differences between summer and winter
hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters
exp: Think Burgundy or Ribera del Duero: short hot summers, cold winters, and real frost risk in spring.

q: A maritime climate, like Bordeaux's, brings:
opts: reliably hot, bone-dry summers year after year
mild temperatures with rainfall spread through the year
no risk of rot or vintage variation
extremely cold winters followed by short, hot summers
exp: Year-round rain means rot risk and real vintage variation — the price of the ocean's mild embrace.

q: A Mediterranean climate features:
opts: warm, dry summers and mild winters
exp: Provence, Tuscany's coast, much of California and South Australia: sunshine and dry summers give reliably ripe grapes.

q: Heavy rain just before harvest can:
opts: swell and dilute the grapes and encourage rot
usefully concentrate the sugars in the berries
exp: Late rain bloats berries with water, diluting flavour, and damp bunches invite grey rot.

q: In very dry regions such as Mendoza, growers commonly:
opts: rely on morning fog for all their water
harvest before the grapes are ripe
add water directly to the fermenting wine
exp: With under 250mm of rain a year, Mendoza depends on Andean meltwater irrigation.

q: As grapes ripen on the vine, sugar levels ___ while acidity ___.
exp: Photosynthesis pumps in sugar while acid is respired away — pick date is a balance between the two.

q: Winter pruning is used to:
opts: warm the vineyard during cold snaps
protect the vine directly against fungal disease and pests
control the number of buds and manage next season's yield
exp: Fewer buds = fewer, more concentrated bunches; pruning is the grower's main lever on quantity vs quality.

q: Removing leaves around the fruit zone (canopy management) helps by:
opts: hiding the ripening grapes from hungry birds and insects
keeping the soil cool and damp
exposing grapes to sun and improving airflow against rot
exp: Sun ripens the bunches while moving air dries them out — a double defence for quality.

q: Phylloxera, the vine-killing louse, is controlled by:
opts: spraying copper sulfate onto the leaves and soil
grafting vines onto resistant American rootstocks
exp: American vine species evolved with phylloxera and resist it — nearly every European vine now grows on their roots.

q: Which is a fungal disease encouraged by damp conditions?
exp: Unwanted botrytis (grey rot) ruins grapes in damp weather — the same fungus that, in the right conditions, becomes noble rot.

q: Compared with warm regions, wines from cool climates generally have:
opts: deeper colour with noticeably heavier tannin
much higher alcohol with jammy, riper fruit
higher acidity, lighter body and lower alcohol
exp: Less heat = less sugar and more retained acid — the fundamental climate equation of wine style.

q: The main advantages of machine harvesting are:
opts: usability on the very steepest slopes
speed and lower cost, plus the option of picking at night
more careful selection of each individual berry picked
gentler handling of whole, unbroken bunches
exp: Machines are fast and cheap and can pick in the cool of night — but hand harvest wins on selection, gentleness and steep terrain.

q: What defines the traditional method used for Champagne?
opts: the second fermentation happens in a sealed tank
a single fermentation is stopped early
the second fermentation happens inside the bottle
CO₂ is injected into the still wine
exp: The bubbles are created — and the wine aged on its lees — in the very bottle you buy.

q: The biscuit and toast flavours of Champagne come from:
opts: fermentation and long aging in heavily toasted oak barrels
the natural flavour of the Glera grape
autolysis — dead yeast breaking down during aging in bottle
exp: Months to years resting on the lees after the second fermentation create the bready, biscuity autolytic notes.

q: What is the purpose of riddling (remuage)?
opts: to collect the yeast sediment in the neck of the bottle
to dissolve the CO₂ from fermentation evenly into the wine
to blend the reserve wines evenly
exp: Bottles are tilted and turned until the lees sit on the crown cap, ready to be removed.

q: What is disgorgement?
opts: pressing the base wine very gently
ejecting the frozen plug of yeast sediment from the bottle
adding the sugar and yeast for the second fermentation
transferring the wine to a pressurised tank
exp: The neck is frozen and the pressure fires out the sediment plug, leaving clear sparkling wine.

q: The dosage added after disgorgement determines the wine's:
exp: This small dose of wine and sugar sets the style, from Brut Nature (none) to Doux (very sweet).

q: Which Champagne label term indicates the SWEETEST style?
exp: The scale runs (driest → sweetest): Brut Nature → Extra Brut → Brut → Extra-Sec → Sec → Demi-Sec → Doux.

q: On a Prosecco label, 'Extra Dry' actually means:
opts: aged under a layer of flor
exp: A famous trap: the historic scale puts Extra Dry (12–17 g/l sugar) above Brut (0–12 g/l) in sweetness.

q: The three main Champagne grapes are:
opts: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris
exp: One white grape and two black grapes make up virtually all Champagne.

q: Blanc de Blancs Champagne is made from:
exp: 'White from whites' — Chardonnay is Champagne's only principal white grape.

q: Blanc de Noirs is:
opts: a white sparkling wine made from black grapes
a red sparkling wine made in Burgundy
a sweet rosé style made by blending
a still white wine from the Côte des Blancs
exp: Pressed gently so no skin colour bleeds in, Pinot Noir and Meunier yield a white wine — 'white from blacks'.

q: Non-vintage (NV) Champagne blends wines from several years mainly to:
exp: Reserve wines smooth over vintage variation so each house's NV tastes recognisably the same every year.

q: Vintage Champagne is made:
opts: by blending the two best recent years together
only from a single declared year's harvest
exp: Houses 'declare' a vintage only when the harvest is outstanding; the wine then ages longer on its lees.

q: Cava is made with which trio of grapes?
exp: Cava uses local Catalan varieties — though made by the same traditional method as Champagne.

q: Cava's production method is:
opts: the tank method used for Prosecco and Asti
the same traditional method used in Champagne
simple carbonation with injected CO₂ gas
exp: Second fermentation in bottle, lees aging, riddling, disgorgement — the full traditional process at a friendlier price.

q: Prosecco tastes fresh and simply fruity (pear, apple) because:
opts: the tank method preserves its fresh primary fruit
the Glera grape is fermented and aged in new oak barrels
exp: The quick second fermentation in tank keeps Glera's fresh orchard fruit front and centre — no biscuity autolysis.

q: Asti differs from most sparkling wines because:
opts: one fermentation is stopped early, keeping natural sweetness
the wine goes through two separate fermentations in bottle
it is made from black grapes only
it must age ten years before release
exp: The Asti method halts one fermentation part-way: natural grape sugar remains, alcohol stays around 7%, and Moscato's florality shines.

q: Crémant d'Alsace, Crémant de Loire and Crémant de Bourgogne are:
opts: French traditional-method sparkling wines made outside Champagne
tank-method sparkling wines made in the same style as Prosecco
German-style Sekt produced under licence in France
lightly sparkling sweet red wines for dessert
exp: 'Crémant' signals traditional-method fizz from French regions beyond Champagne, using local grapes.

q: South Africa's traditional-method sparkling wine is labelled:
exp: Méthode Cap Classique (MCC) is South Africa's answer to Champagne, often from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

q: Why is tank-method sparkling wine generally cheaper to make than traditional-method?
opts: the neutral grapes it uses cost far less to grow
no second addition of yeast is needed for the bubbles
the second fermentation happens in one large tank
the tanks add oak-like flavour without the cost of barrels
exp: No riddling, no disgorgement, no years of cellaring — the tank method is fast and scalable.

q: Which sparkling wine is intensely floral, grapey, sweet and around 7% alcohol?
exp: That is Asti's signature: Moscato's perfume, natural sweetness, gentle fizz and low alcohol.

q: Port stays sweet because grape spirit is added:
opts: just before the wine is bottled
after the fermentation has finished completely
exp: Fortifying to ~20% mid-ferment stops the yeast dead, leaving natural grape sugar in the wine.

q: Ruby Port is:
opts: deep in colour with fresh black fruit, bottled young
a white wine style of Port
amber and nutty after decades of aging in barrel
pale, bone dry and always served well chilled
exp: Brief protective aging preserves Ruby's youthful colour and primary blackberry fruit.

q: Late Bottled Vintage (LBV) Port is:
opts: a blend of many different years aged for up to four decades
wine from a single year, aged about 4–6 years before bottling
a lighter style made from white grapes
an unfortified red from the Douro
exp: LBV offers single-vintage character that is ready to drink on release — no decades of bottle age required.

q: A 10- or 20-Year-Old Tawny Port gets its nut and caramel character from:
opts: long oxidative aging in small oak barrels
a layer of flor yeast on its surface
exp: Years in barrel with gentle oxygen exposure fade the colour to tawny and build walnut, caramel and dried-fruit flavours.

q: Vintage Port is:
opts: aged for at least forty years in barrel before its release
made only in declared years and matured for decades in bottle
produced in every single year as required by law
a sweetened, filtered style of Ruby
exp: Bottled unfiltered after ~2 years in wood, Vintage Port does its real aging in bottle — and throws a heavy sediment.

q: The base grape for the dry styles of Sherry is:
exp: Neutral Palomino is the canvas; the magic comes from flor or oxidative aging in the solera.

q: What is 'flor'?
opts: the fine cellar filter used just before bottling
the traditional type of oak cask used for aging Oloroso
the Andalusian technique of drying grapes in the sun
a protective layer of yeast on the wine's surface
exp: Flor shields Fino from oxidation while adding its signature bready, almond tang.

q: Fino Sherry is:
opts: pale and bone dry with almond notes, served chilled
nearly black and syrupy sweet with fig flavours
red, tannic and served at room temperature
amber and nutty from long, deliberate oxidation
exp: Aged entirely under flor, Fino is the palest, freshest, driest Sherry style.

q: Manzanilla is:
opts: a light fortified wine made in Portugal's Douro Valley
an oxidatively aged style, closely related to Oloroso
a sweet, dark style made entirely from sun-dried grapes
a Fino-style Sherry from coastal Sanlúcar, with a salty tang
exp: The humid seaside air of Sanlúcar de Barrameda keeps flor thick year-round — Manzanilla is the lightest Sherry of all.

q: Oloroso never develops flor because:
opts: its cellars are kept too cold for the yeast to grow
it is fortified to around 17%, too strong for the yeast
its casks are sealed completely airtight against oxygen
it is made from black grapes
exp: Fortifying above ~17% kills flor before it starts, so Oloroso ages in contact with air — hence its walnut and toffee richness.

q: Amontillado Sherry combines:
opts: no barrel aging at all, only bottle age
purely oxidative aging from the very beginning
biological aging under flor for its whole life
aging under flor first, then oxidative aging
exp: Amontillado begins life as a Fino; when the flor dies, oxygen takes over — giving a style between Fino and Oloroso.

q: PX Sherry is intensely sweet because:
opts: its fermentation is never allowed to begin at all
the flor yeast produces sweetness as it grows
sugar syrup is blended into the wine before bottling
its grapes are sun-dried, concentrating their sugar
exp: Sun-drying Pedro Ximénez grapes creates a near-black, syrupy wine tasting of raisins, figs and coffee.

q: Cream Sherry is:
opts: a naturally sweet style of Fino
exp: Cream Sherries take rich oxidative Oloroso and sweeten it, usually with PX.

q: The solera system used in Jerez:
opts: keeps every vintage strictly separate until bottling
is the traditional way of drying grapes on straw mats
is the machine that riddles sparkling wine bottles
blends younger wines into older ones for consistency
exp: Wine drawn for bottling is replaced by slightly younger wine, cascading down the scale — no bottle is a single vintage.

q: Because Sherry is fortified AFTER fermentation, its base wine is naturally:
exp: All the sugar is fermented out first; sweet Sherries get their sugar from PX/Moscatel additions or dried grapes.

q: Sherry's vineyards famously grow on which bright white soil?
exp: Spongy white albariza soaks up winter rain and feeds Palomino through the baking Andalusian summer.

q: Which fortified wine is typically served chilled and drunk young and fresh?
exp: Fino fades fast once open — serve it cold and finish the bottle like a white wine.

q: 'Trocken' on a German label means:
exp: Trocken = dry; halbtrocken = off-dry.

q: 'Halbtrocken' indicates a wine that is:
exp: Literally 'half-dry' — a touch of balancing sweetness, common in German Riesling.

q: Germany's Prädikat levels rank wines by:
opts: the final alcohol content of the finished wine
how long the wine spent aging in oak barrels
the ripeness (sugar level) of the grapes at harvest
the altitude and steepness of the vineyard site
exp: From Kabinett up to Trockenbeerenauslese, each step means riper (sweeter) grapes were picked.

q: Which Prädikat level is the LIGHTEST, from the least ripe grapes?
exp: Kabinett is the entry rung of the ripeness ladder — delicate, low in alcohol, often off-dry.

q: 'Spätlese' literally means:
exp: Picked later than Kabinett, Spätlese grapes are riper, giving more concentration and body.

q: Which Prädikat category, made from shrivelled botrytis berries, is the rarest and sweetest of all?
exp: Don't let 'Trocken(dry)-beeren-auslese' fool you: TBA is the sweetest, rarest Prädikat of all.

q: Rioja Crianza requires a minimum of:
opts: 5 years of aging, with at least 2 years in oak
2 years aging, with at least 1 year in oak
exp: Crianza is the first rung: 2 years total including 1 in barrel (for reds).

q: Rioja's aging categories from youngest to oldest are:
exp: Each step up means longer total and oak aging — Gran Reserva reds need 5 years including 2 in oak.

q: Spain's elite DOCa status is held by:
exp: DOCa (Denominación de Origen Calificada) has been granted to just two regions.

q: Italy's top classification tier is:
exp: DOCG — Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita — sits above DOC, with tighter rules and a tasting guarantee.

q: 'Classico' on a bottle of Soave or Chianti means the wine is from:
opts: grapes given extra aging in classic oak casks
the original heartland zone of the region
an estate that bottles its own wine
exp: When appellations expanded, the historic core kept the 'Classico' name — often the best hillside sites.

q: 'Riserva' on an Italian label indicates:
opts: a single-vineyard bottling from the estate's best plot
a wine that is always sweet
longer aging before release than the standard wine
exp: Riserva requirements vary by DOC/DOCG but always mean extended aging, often with higher minimum alcohol.

q: AOC (Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée) on a French label is:
opts: a government rating of the wine's sweetness level
France's PDO tier, with strict rules on area and methods
a private brand name owned by a négociant house
official proof that the wine was aged in oak barrels
exp: AOC/AC is the traditional French expression of the EU's PDO system.

q: The key difference between PDO and PGI wines is:
opts: PGI wines are always higher in quality and price than PDO wines
PDO status applies only to red wines, PGI only to whites
there is no practical difference between the two
PDO: smaller area, stricter rules; PGI: larger and more flexible
exp: PGI (e.g. Pays d'Oc) allows more varieties and higher yields across a bigger territory.

q: For an EU wine labelled with a single grape variety, the wine must contain at least:
exp: The 85% minimum also applies to a stated vintage year.

q: In Burgundy, 'Grand Cru' refers to:
opts: any wine from vines over 50 years old
exp: Burgundy classifies the LAND: Grand Cru vineyards like Montrachet carry only the vineyard name on the label.

q: In Bordeaux, 'Grand Cru Classé' refers to:
opts: single top-ranked vineyard sites, as in Burgundy
a legal minimum aging requirement before release
exp: Bordeaux ranks producers, not plots — the famous 1855 list still defines the Médoc hierarchy.

q: The word 'Reserve' on a Californian label legally means:
opts: nothing — it has no legal definition in the USA
five years of total aging including two in barrel
the wine is from a single vineyard
a legal minimum of two years of aging in oak
exp: Unlike Rioja's Reserva or Italy's Riserva, 'Reserve' in the USA (and many other countries) is unregulated marketing language.

q: 'Vieilles Vignes' on a French label means:
exp: Old vines yield less fruit with more concentration — though the term has no strict legal definition.

q: 'Sur Lie' on a Muscadet label means the wine was:
opts: fermented spontaneously with wild vineyard yeasts
bottled directly off its yeast lees, gaining texture
harvested late for extra ripeness and sweetness
matured in new oak barrels for added richness
exp: A winter resting on the lees gives Muscadet extra body and sometimes a light prickle of CO₂.

q: 'Vendanges Tardives' on an Alsace label means:
opts: a wine fortified with grape spirit
late-harvested, extra-ripe grapes — usually rich and sweet
an early-picked style that is always bone dry and light
exp: Late harvest concentrates sugar — Alsace VT wines from Gewurztraminer or Riesling are opulent and honeyed.

q: If a wine makes your mouth water profusely, it is high in:
exp: Salivation is the tell-tale response to acidity — the higher the acid, the more your mouth waters.

q: Tannin is perceived in the mouth as:
opts: a burning warmth in the throat and chest
a mouth-watering tang along the sides of the tongue
a drying, grippy sensation on the gums and cheeks
a rich sweetness felt on the tip of the tongue
exp: Tannin binds with saliva — the drying grip you feel after strong black tea. (Burning warmth = alcohol.)

q: 'Body' describes:
opts: the overall intensity of the wine's aromas
the depth and intensity of the wine's colour
the weight and fullness of the wine in the mouth
how sweet the wine tastes on the palate
exp: Body is the overall mouth-filling impression, driven by alcohol, sugar, extract and tannin.

q: The 'finish' of a wine refers to:
opts: the polish of the bottle's label
how long its flavours linger after swallowing
the most recent vintage released by a producer
exp: A long, pleasant finish is one of the strongest simple indicators of quality.

q: Which group are all PRIMARY aromas?
exp: Primary aromas come from the grape itself; the other groups come from winemaking (secondary) and age (tertiary).

q: Butter, biscuit and vanilla in a wine are examples of:
opts: typical signs of a faulty wine
exp: Butter = MLF, biscuit = lees, vanilla = oak: all winemaker's choices, hence 'secondary'.

q: Leather, mushroom and dried fruit in an older red indicate:
opts: primary fruit characters at their very freshest
flavours picked up from stainless steel tanks
a wine badly spoiled by cork taint (TCA)
exp: These are the rewards of graceful aging — fresh fruit slowly transforms into savoury, earthy complexity.

q: As red wines age, their colour:
opts: turns a brighter shade of pink at the rim
stays exactly the same for decades
fades toward garnet and tawny with a paler rim
deepens steadily to an opaque, inky purple
exp: Reds lose colour with age while whites gain it — a key visual clue when assessing a wine.

q: A pale lemon colour in a white wine usually suggests:
exp: Whites deepen toward gold and amber over time — pale lemon says youth (or careful protective winemaking).

q: Sweetness in food makes a wine taste:
opts: drier, more bitter and more acidic
exp: Sugar in food 'hardens' wine — which is why the wine should always be sweeter than the dish.

q: Umami-rich foods (mushrooms, aged cheese, soy) make wine seem:
opts: noticeably softer, rounder and more mellow
much lower in alcohol and lighter
sweeter, fruitier and fuller in body
more drying, more bitter and more acidic
exp: Like sweetness, umami emphasises a wine's hard edges — tread carefully with tannic reds.

q: Salt in food generally makes wine taste:
exp: Salt is the most wine-friendly element on the plate — it flatters nearly everything in the glass.

q: High-acid foods such as a vinaigrette salad are best matched with:
opts: a soft wine with gentle, low acidity
a wine with equally high acidity
exp: Acid in food makes wine taste softer and flatter — a high-acid wine keeps its freshness alongside.

q: Chilli heat in food makes a wine seem:
opts: cooler, lighter and more refreshing overall
lower in acidity but otherwise unchanged
more alcoholic, more astringent and less fruity
exp: Capsaicin amplifies alcohol burn — low-alcohol, slightly sweet wines (like off-dry Riesling) handle spice best.

q: A rich, fatty or oily dish is refreshed best by a wine with:
exp: Acidity cuts through fat and cleanses the palate — think Champagne with fried food or Riesling with pork belly.

q: Rare steak works well with a tannic red because:
opts: the tannins turn into sugar with hot food
the meat's protein makes the tannins feel softer
the acid in the meat cancels out the wine's acidity
exp: Protein binds tannin, smoothing the wine — the classic logic behind steak and young Cabernet.

q: A wine served with dessert should ideally be:
opts: at least as sweet as the dessert itself
completely dry to contrast with the sugar
exp: If the dish out-sweetens the wine, the wine tastes thin and sour — hence Sauternes with tarte tatin.

q: Salty blue cheese with sweet Port is a classic pairing because:
opts: the sweet–salty contrast flatters wine and cheese alike
the pairing masks the Port's high alcohol completely
the Port's tannins soften the texture of the cheese rind
blue cheese removes all bitterness from wine
exp: Salt softens the wine while the wine's sweetness balances the cheese's punch — opposites attracting.

q: A wine affected by cork taint (TCA) smells of:
exp: TCA mutes the fruit and adds a wet-cardboard mustiness — the fault behind the term 'corked'.

q: A wine spoiled by oxidation typically:
opts: smells strongly of damp cardboard and musty cellars
looks brownish and tastes flat, like bruised apples
fizzes when it should be still
exp: Too much oxygen browns the colour and dulls fresh fruit into stale, sherry-like flavours.

q: The ideal conditions for long-term wine storage are:
opts: anywhere, as temperature does not matter
a cool, constant 10–15°C in the dark
exp: Cool, constant and dark: heat and temperature swings age wine prematurely.

q: Bottles sealed with natural cork are stored on their side so that:
opts: more bottles fit in the rack
the cork stays moist and airtight
exp: A dry cork shrinks and lets oxygen creep in; contact with the wine keeps it swollen and sealed.

q: Besides temperature, stored wine should be protected from:
exp: UV light and constant vibration both degrade wine over time — hence dark, still cellars.

q: Full-bodied red wines are best served at:
exp: Just below old-fashioned 'room temperature' — warm enough to open the aromas without the alcohol turning soupy.

q: Light-bodied reds such as Beaujolais are best served:
exp: A light chill sharpens their fresh red fruit — one of the few reds that loves the fridge door.

q: Sparkling wine should be served:
opts: at any temperature — it makes no difference
exp: Cold keeps the mousse fine and the wine crisp; a warm bottle gushes and tastes flabby.

q: Why is Vintage Port decanted before serving?
opts: to add oxygen, which raises the alcohol level
to separate the wine from its heavy sediment
to chill the wine more rapidly
exp: Decades of bottle age throw a thick deposit — careful pouring off the sediment leaves the wine clear.

q: A vacuum stopper system helps an opened bottle by:
exp: Less oxygen in the bottle means the wine stays fresh for a few extra days.
